newsitem.title: UK: MOTOR RACING-PAST COURT ACTIONS AFTER MOTOR RACING DEATHS.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-PAST COURT ACTIONS AFTER MOTOR RACING DEATHS.

text.p: Williams Formula One team chief Frank Williams and five other people will go on trial in February accused of manslaughter over the death of Ayrton Senna during the 1994 San Marino Grand Prix.
No criminal convictions have arisen from previous court inquiries into motor racing deaths.
Following is a list of previous court actions stemming from high-profile motor racing accidents:

Italian Grand Prix, 1961 - German Wolfgang von Trips died at Monza following a collision with Jim Clark's Lotus. Fourteen spectators were also killed in the accident when the car plunged off the track. Although Clark was initially blamed for the crash, the official inquiry did not find him guilty.

Italian Grand Prix, 1970 -- Austrian Jochen Rindt lost his life during the final qualifying session at Monza when his Lotus went off the track as he braked for the Parabolica Curve. The car was impounded by investigators and the inquiry went on for several years, although without an eventual conclusion. In 1971 Lotus were worried about possible litigation and travelled to the race with only one car, entered under a different team called 'Worldwide Racing'. Team boss Colin Chapman did not travel to Italy.

Austrian Grand Prix, 1975 -- American Mark Donohue died from a brain haemorrhage following an accident, caused by tyre failure, during the warm-up at the Osterreichring. His widow took legal action against Goodyear and won her case, only to lose on appeal. The tyre company came close to quitting motor racing altogether.

Italian Grand Prix, 1978 -- Swede Ronnie Peterson suffered severe leg injuries in a start line accident at the Monza race. Italian Formula One rookie Riccardo Patrese was widely criticised over the crash and it took many months for the official inquiry to clear him of any blame.

Investigations into other deaths, even in Italy, have not gone as far as the courts. Last month Bologna prosecutor Maurizio Passarini, who has led the prosecutions into Senna's death, won leave from an examining judge to drop proceedings against five people investigated in connection with the death of Austrian Roland Ratzenberger in an accident the day before the crash that claimed Senna's life.
